Action Plan:
- Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.
1) Continue knee ice therapy as part of self-care; apply ice regularly and after activity to reduce swelling and pain; avoid heat on acute injury.
2) Modify running program to reduce load; continue marathon training but ease up on long runs; if pain prevents continued running, avoid pushing through pain.
3) Pain/anti-inflammatory management: Continue ibuprofen for current symptoms as needed; a slightly stronger NSAID will be prescribed for regular use, but not concurrently with ibuprofen; take with food; dose/route/frequency of the new NSAID not documented. Pharmacy will receive the prescription.
4) Knee evaluation and imaging plan: Arrange a physiotherapist assessment for a comprehensive knee examination; based on findings, consider knee imaging (e.g., MRI) to evaluate cartilage/other intra-articular pathology.
5) Referrals and access: If wait times are long, an in-clinic appointment can be scheduled; a formal referral to physiotherapy will be placed.
6) Red-flag instructions: If persistent swelling, warmth, redness, fever, or if the knee completely locks or cannot bend/stretch, contact urgent care or return to evaluation promptly.
7) (No COVID-19 vaccine update mentioned in the encounter.)

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint: Right knee pain with clicking after increased workouts; difficulty running longer distances.
- Onset and course: Symptoms began about 2 weeks ago; pain typically starts after about 20 minutes of running (roughly mile 2–3); pain worsens with knee bending and running; occasional “giving way” sensation but not a true instability.
- Pain character and location: Mid-knee pain with occasional migration toward the right side of the knee; clicking on movement; transient swelling after the first run that resolved with ice.
- Aggravating/alleviating factors: Pain with running and abdominal/hip-related movement; ice reduces symptoms; rest reduces symptoms temporarily.
- Functional impact: Can still straighten and fully flex the knee; pain limits endurance for longer runs; no need for assistance with stairs or walking at the moment.
- Other symptoms: Occasional tingling in the right toes after a run; no persistent redness, warmth, fever; no locking when sitting or standing; no major involvement of the left knee.
- Past medical history: Prior ice-hockey knee bruise several months ago; past ED visit for severe UTI mistaken for kidney stones; generally good health otherwise.
- Medications: Ibuprofen as needed (max ~400 mg per dose); also uses Aleve (naproxen) occasionally without documented dose; Vitamin D; Melatonin; Xanax occasionally; cannabis use; Lasik in the past.
- Allergies: None reported.
- Social: Actively training for a marathon (June); high activity level; resides in London; uses cannabis; no heavy alcohol use described.
- Other: No significant back pain or widespread joint swelling; no persistent symptoms when sedentary.

Objective:
- Vitals: Not provided in transcript.
- Right knee exam: Not all details documented in the transcript, but patient reports:
  - ROM: Full extension and full flexion.
  - Current swelling: Not swollen at present.
  - Pain with movement: Pain develops with running and with flexion/extension; clicking observed with movement.
  - Instability/lock: Patient denies significant instability or locking at rest; no current locking.
  - Palpation tenderness: Not clearly described; patient reported prior transient effusion.
- Other systems: No systemic symptoms reported.

Assessment & Plan:
1) Right knee pain with mechanical symptoms (clicking) in a runner.
- Likelihood and differential (from DDx, consistent with transcript):
  - Meniscal tear (traumatic or degenerative) — High
  - Patellofemoral pain syndrome / chondromalacia patellae — High
  - Osteoarthritis of the knee — Medium
  - Iliotibial band syndrome — Medium
  - Traumatic ligament injuries (ACL/MCL) — Low
- Investigations planned:
  - Initial: comprehensive knee assessment by a physiotherapist
  - Imaging: knee imaging (e.g., MRI) if exam suggests intra-articular pathology or if symptoms persist/worsen
- Treatment planned:
  - Ice therapy continued
  - Activity modification (reduce running load)
  - NSAID management: continue Ibuprofen as needed; start a stronger NSAID for regular use with food; avoid combining with Ibuprofen
  - Referral to physiotherapy for targeted assessment and rehabilitation
- Referrals: Refer to physiotherapist; consider imaging if indicated after exam

2) Transient paresthesias in the right toes after running.
- Assessment: Paresthesias post-exercise; current data insufficient to establish a specific neurovascular or other diagnosis.
- Plan: Monitor symptoms; no immediate imaging or interventions planned unless symptoms persist, worsen, or are accompanied by other concerning signs.
